back: the study of techniques used for encryption and secure communications.
a person who studies and analyzes cryptography and builds protocols that stop unauthorized users from reading private messages.
the study of how to crack encryption algorithms or their implementations.
a set of rules (an algorithm) for how to perform encryption or decryption.
readable data before encryption.
encrypted output.
the instructions or secret value that tells the cipher how to encrypt and decrypt.
all possible values for a key. A bigger key is more secure but uses more CPU.
generating, verifying, exchanging, storing, and destroying keys at the end of their lifetime.
the sender cannot deny sending the data.
replaces one character with another. The exact substitution method is the key.
like substitution, but uses multiple alphabets and switches between them on a trigger character in the message.
rearranges the letters. Example: "This is secret" written top to bottom, left to right, then read from the top right going clockwise and spiraling inward gives RETCSIHTSSEI.

a key used only once, the same length as the message (32-bit message, 32-bit pad). Each pad bit is combined with a message bit to make the ciphertext. The receiver must also have the pad. Not the same as a one-time password.
symmetric cipher that works on a fixed group of bits called a block (for example, 64-bit plaintext block in, 64-bit ciphertext block out). Adds padding when there is not enough data to fill a block.
symmetric cipher that encrypts plaintext one bit at a time against the key stream (cipher digit stream). Output is a ciphertext stream. No padding, so slightly less overhead than a block cipher.
the same key encrypts and decrypts. Fast and low CPU, so it is used for bulk data encryption.
uses two mathematically linked keys, a public key and a private key. High CPU cost, so used sparingly for authentication and generating keying material.
one public key and one private key that work together. What one encrypts, only the other decrypts.
published and available to anyone.
known only to the device that owns the key pair. Never shared.
a method used to verify data integrity.
a one-way function that takes a block of data and creates a small fixed-size hash value. The same data always produces the same hash.
the fixed-length output of a hash function.
it is not realistically possible to produce the same hash from different data.
two different inputs produce the same hash value. Possible because hash inputs are unlimited in length but outputs are fixed.
an attacker finds or creates two inputs with the same hash. Undermines digital signatures and certificates.
an attacker creates a message that has a specific hash value.
a hash that includes a secret key in its calculation, so only someone with the key can create or verify it. Gives a message authentication code (MAC) for integrity verification.
a hash encrypted with the sender's private key and attached to the data. Provides authentication, data integrity, and nonrepudiation.
symmetric block cipher.
symmetric block cipher.
symmetric block cipher.
symmetric block cipher.
symmetric block ciphers.
symmetric algorithms.
asymmetric. Main use today is authentication (RSA digital signatures). Also called PKCS #1.

asymmetric key exchange that lets two devices negotiate and establish shared secret keying material over an untrusted network. The algorithm is asymmetric, but the keys it produces are symmetric (used with 3DES, AES).
asymmetric encryption system based on the DH exchange.
asymmetric. Developed by the U.S. National Security Agency.
asymmetric.
elliptic curve variant of DSA. Replaces RSA signatures in NGE. DSA has been a standard since 1994.
elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman. Replaces DH key exchange in NGE.
128-bit hash. Broken and should be avoided.
160-bit hash. Outdated, has known vulnerabilities, use is discouraged.
digests from 224 to 512 bits.

the recommended SHA version. Uses a sponge construction, output sizes 224 to 512 bits, and sequential, parallel, and tree modes. Designed to resist all known attacks, including collision and pre-image.
fast, flexible hash for high-speed processing of large data with strong security. An alternative to SHA-2 and MD5.
512-bit hash, resistant to various attacks.
AES mode of operation in NGE.
U.S. government's recommended set of cryptographic standards. Approved for classified information at secret and top-secret levels. Cisco helped develop some of it.
the Suite B algorithms for authenticated encryption, digital signatures, key establishment, and hashing.
developing and deploying algorithms that can withstand attacks from powerful quantum computers.
post-quantum suite made of Kyber and Dilithium. Both rely on module lattice problems.
key-encapsulation mechanism (KEM). Secure against chosen-ciphertext attacks (IND-CCA2).
digital signature algorithm. Secure against existential forgery under adaptive chosen-message attacks (EUF-CMA).
other post-quantum algorithms.
suite of protocols and algorithms that protect IP packets at Layer 3. Used for remote-access and site-to-site VPNs.
IPsec method that can do all IPsec features, including encryption.
IPsec method that does most IPsec features except encryption, so it is rarely used.
a shared secret used only for authentication, similar to a password.
does much of the negotiation and management IPsec needs.
IPsec protection against replayed packets.
browser-based encryption and server authentication over HTTPS. Supported by almost every browser.
the successor to SSL and the preferred method of encrypted communication.

a set of identities, roles, policies, and actions for the creation, use, management, distribution, and revocation of public and private keys. Binds public keys to the identities of people, applications, and organizations.
a trusted computer or entity that creates, signs, and issues digital certificates.
an electronic document that identifies a device or person and holds its public key, signed by a CA.
identifies the CA and contains the CA's public key. Its subject is the CA itself.
identifies a client (a web server, a router) and contains that host's public key.
a CA that the root CA delegates to issue identity certificates to clients.
a root CA signs subordinate CA certificates, and the subordinates issue client certificates.
a horizontal trust relationship between two CAs so clients of either can trust the other's signatures.
the hash of a certificate. **Thumbprint algorithm**: the hash algorithm used.
checking a certificate's hash through another channel, such as a phone call to the CA admins.
getting and trusting the root CA certificate.
requesting and receiving an identity certificate from a CA.
list of revoked certificate serial numbers. "The naughty list."
asks for the status of one certificate instead of downloading the whole CRL.
Cisco-developed protocol (with other vendors) that automates requesting and installing certificates. Not an open standard.
series of standards for directory services and how directories are organized. The basis of Microsoft Active Directory.
the widely accepted standard for digital certificates. Uses X.500 naming.
